For all of us who don't understand the rally language, here is a quick beginners guide:

L, R: Left corner ahead, right corner ahead.

1,2,3,4,5,6: The number refers to the severity of a corner ahead. The spectrum goes from 1, referring to a slower, first-gear hairpin, to 6, which refers to a flat-out, sixth-gear sweeper.

+, -: Modifiers that adjust the above numbers slightly, giving the driver more detailed information.

: Opens and tightens, two notations that help describe an upcoming corner's intricacies.

40,50,60 ... 200: Numbers from 40 to 200 represent distance (in yards) between instructions and features on the rally stage road.

&: "And" represents a distance shorter than 40 yards.

->: "Into" represents a very short distance that requires the driver to transition directly from one action to another.

Cr: A "crest" is something you can't see over or a feature that will likely unsettle the car.

Jmp: A "jump" will make the car come off the ground.

/: When you go "over" something, you need to take action while going over or through a rally stage feature.

OC: A corner is "off-camber."

Slippy: Slippery section of road.

Grip: Section of road with a lot of grip.

Care: Difficult road ahead.

!: Caution means there's a higher-than-normal probability there could be a crash.

!!: Double caution means there's a higher-than-normal probability there could be a crash and that crashing will total your rally car.

!!!: Triple caution means there's a higher-than-normal probability there could be a crash that could kill you.

Hope this helps :)

There’s a lot this game does right and there’s a few things it does wrong but the issue is these few things are either major or "in the player's face", so to speak.

For the purposes of those reading, I'm reviewing GotY DIRT Rally 2.0 which comes with the various season DLCs and the "FLAT OUT" DLC. 

[h1]Game Modes[/h1]
There are two primary modes that come with the game: Rally and Rallycross which both have a single player and multiplayer feature. Rally is your run of the mill point to point time attack style of racing where you run through various locations and see if you're faster than your competition.

Every two stages you can enter a service area and get setup changes and car repairs. Repairs are offered as either a standard repair (fully fix the part), quick fix (cheap and fast repair, but leads to the part being un-repairable and diminishes quicker) or a full on replacement of the part. Repairs are also influenced by your expandable and upgradable team mechanics.

In addition to costing you time, with a limit of 30 minutes to complete your repairs, they also cost money. Yes, it’s frustrating you run out of money and the game forces choice upon the player, but that’s what makes the game fun and interesting – rally is a very harsh motorsport after all and your driving style needs to weigh speed and risk of damage. Even if you run out of money, you can just do a quick rallycross event or online event and get some quick cash, complete those repairs and continue your rally as if your brief financial worries didn't exist in the first place. Good addition.

Rallycross mode hasn’t changed much since the original game. You and 4-6 other drivers compete on a circuit in a traditional race with each driver having to take one “joker” lap, that is use a section of the course which is a bit longer than the normal course or face a hefty penalty. Events are divided into heats deciding drivers qualifying for a semi-final and then a final. 

Readers who have played the first game will notice that I didn’t mention hillclimb. Well, we have Polyphony to thank for that. Less said about exclusivity deals especially in this day and age the better. But let's now talk about what is in the game:

[h1]Locations[/h1]
The game has 7 new rallies to try with the original 6 available via DLC. These new rallies are:

Argentina – Gravel, narrow for the most part and very technical. But this is such a boring rally. The stages don’t really give the driver a chance to create a flow through the corners. The roads are so narrow you can’t pendulum turn and are forced to spam your handbrake just to get rotation at such low speeds. Either get rid of this or make it more open with sections that stretch the cars legs, so to speak, more prominent. 

Australia – Very much in the mould of previous Australian rallies shipped with the game. Thick gravel with a mix of high speed and technical bits. Always been a solid addition to the game since the 1990s.

New Zealand – As above. Perhaps more technical. But perhaps the gravel is less abrasive? There isn’t much to say about it apart from what’s mentioned for Australia. There’s only so much you can do with gravel roads, I guess.

Poland – Poland is a bit like Germany but the “openness” of sorts that you get there is replaced with crests in awkward places and sections of road seeing you go at the car’s limit whilst flanked by trees. And I love it. Good stuff, Codies – a fun addition to the DR roster.

Spain – This is basically Monaco but without the ice and less hairpins. Decent addition.

USA – A slow grower on me. Based in New England in the autumn, this is probably similar to Poland but with less tarmac and the straight sections are much less intimidating. Still a fun rally.

Perth and Kinross [DLC] – I find this to be a narrower version of Finland. The straight sections with both trees and tree stumps uncomfortably close to the road and the technical bits test the driver. In my top 3 rallies in the game.
The base game comes with eight licensed World Rallycross Tracks with Holjes, and Hell making it from DR to DR2 base game. Silverstone, Mettet, Barcelona, Trois-Rivieres, Loheac Bretagne and Montalgre completing the list. Further DLC introduces Bikernieki, Estering, Yas Snorina, Lydden Hill (DR1 clone) and Killarney.
I’ll say I haven’t played enough of the rallycross to give you a fair assessment.

[h1]Cars[/h1]
Cars are pretty much as per the original with the 2010s class gone and replaced by the R5 category which shares some manufacturer presence with the original game. Added as well is the Kartcross Rallycross cars and Rally GT class which has Grand Tourers like the V8 Vantage and Porsche 911 if the 80s RWD cars didn’t have enough on power oversteer for you. But all your other favourites from Subaru, Mitsubishi, Ford, Lancia, VW, Audi and Peugeot (to name a few) are all featured.

Notably Toyota are still excluded from the game but with that the car roster is actually pretty good with at least one car in the full roster appealing to everyone. 

[h1]Conclusion, gripes/ideas[/h1]
Again, this is a solid title all in all and would recommend to people into racing games but maybe are getting tired of the whole driving ‘round in circles shtick so this game maybe of interest to you!I felt the major problem with the original was a lack of content and if you include for all the DLC there’s over twice the rallies which is a nice and certainly takes a lot longer for the player to learn the stages so massive kudos to Codemasters on that one. 

I must say, I’ve been more critical of this game purely because the original set a high bar for me and what to expect from a sequel and just want this series to do well. Anyway, with all that said time to get into my gripes:

Still putting a massive red cross against charging players for DLC of existing stages with minimal effort going into them. I mean, if you want people to be happy to fork out for the DLC of DR1 content that maybe add an extra route so there’s new stuff to explore. People don’t like being charged for stuff they’ve already played – this isn’t your yearly Formula 1 release.

Pace notes – Add a tool where players can edit pace notes for stages! I shouldn’t have to play a memory game on every stage because the co-driver has forgotten to mention that big tree on the exit that can cause terminal damage or that “5 right” which is actually a 3 right. Pace notes are just as important as car setups. Doesn’t even have to be complicated, just a simple 2D map of the stage showing where the call from the co-driver is triggered and what exactly he says. When you’re done click “test stage” and drive the stage. Having a simple slider for earlier or later co-driver calls isn’t good enough as you expand the amount of track players have to remember.

Setups – I really miss the sliders in the original game. Bring them back as I’m a setup pleb that doesn’t speak in exact terms as to how I want stuff done. Being able to go “ah yeah, a tick softer should be better” was a good introduction to players who find the setup menu intimidating and confusing.

Restarts – Originally, you had a credit reward if you used 5 or less restarts over the rally. Now you get 5 restarts and that’s it? Well, it would be but you can circumvent this by just quitting to the main menu and loading back in: rendering the restart limit pointless and creating needless tedium. Just bring back the credit bonus system and let the player decide if they want to limit restarts like in Dirt Rally.

The Game Size – 107GB for everything which is nuts. I appreciate more content means more space, but this is the kind of size which would make Flight Sims blush. As the game expands and gets more complex, Codemasters should look into how they can optimise their file sizes for future releases.

After getting 100% on this game, I'd give Dirt Rally 2.0 a thumbs up but with a [TRIPLE CAUTION] because despite the game being technically solid with what it does, I can't bring myself to recommend it to anyone who isn't looking for a severely punishing racing experience.

I initially hated this game. In the Rally mode cars felt terrible, tracks were annoyingly complex, events took hours to complete and there was no excitement to be found in any of the presentation to even pretend this game was supposed to be in any way fun. I thought the Rally Cross mode would spice things up, and while I found it less frustrating, by the end of each event I felt unfulfilled and empty. It didn't help that there is absolutely no reason for this game to be always online and the prospect of losing progress because of that loomed in the back of my mind the entire time I progressed further. Crash after crash, restart after restart, I was having an absolutely miserable time. Had I known it was going to be this way I would have never picked up this game.

Despite that, the completionist in me pushed on. I decided to pick off what achievements I could before I couldn't stand playing this game any longer. Most were easy, but some would take several, sometimes dozens of hours to obtain.

At no point did this game get more fun for me, However, I did gradually get better at it.

What I would consider the most difficult achievement in the game, "...Flatout", requires you to go through the Colin Mcrae Career mode, which is a series of 30 challenges you have to complete on the hardest difficulty. Each one requires near perfection from you in order to complete them. Through determination and gritted teeth I would lock in and spend dozens upon dozens of hours beating these challenges. In some cases I would even punch the air in satisfaction after completing a challenge I though was insurmountable.

I bring this up because this was the mode that pushed me beyond what I thought I was capable of. I can't say the process of earning this achievement was enjoyable, It was an absolute endurance test. However the feeling I had after finally obtaining it wasn't nothing. I was not the same driver I was when I started this game and because of that, Dirt Rally 2.0 had earned my respect.

That being said, I don't think I'll be playing this game again out of choice. I would much rather play a game that cared more about me having actual fun. Though I hear the VR experience in this game is exceptional and I can see that, so I may come back to this game if I ever decide to get a VR headset.

This game isn't for the faint of heart. Only those looking for a big challenge, or the most masochistic of achievement hunters should consider picking up this game. If you're into more forgivable arcade racing games like me, perhaps consider skipping this one.

Oh, and for the record, I played on keyboard. So maybe that's why I mostly hated this game.

Generally speaking I am not a racing gamer.  I am not that interested in cars or racing.  That said, every once in awhile I get this desire to play a racing game.  The last one I played was one of the Forza games.  I really didn't enjoy it that much.  This game is different though, and I REALLY like it.

When I bought this game I did not know what "Rally" meant.  I just thought it looked cool having cars that raced on gravel roads as opposed to on a tarmac circuit.  When I started playing I was very puzzled as to why I was getting verbal commands from a co-driver, and for a few minutes I regretted my purchase because I was very confused as to what I had gotten myself into.  After some time though, I realized what was going on, and I love it.  I really enjoy this kind of racing where you are not simply doing laps around a circuit with other cars, but are racing at breakneck speeds through unpredictable terrain with a co-driver giving you verbal commands as to what turns are coming up.

I have picked it up and put it down a couple times, but I have gotten into this racing game like no other racing game I've played.  I still know next to nothing about cars and I don't understand much about the cars in the game other than the difference between real wheel drive, front wheel drive, and four wheel drive.  That said, I'm having a blast with it.

The sound design in this game is top notch.  It's even better than the graphics, which is saying something because the graphics are beautiful.  The engine sounds, tire squeals, the sound of gravel under your tires, everything is so PERFECT.  The sound design is so good that you can hear things going wrong with your car before the co-driver says so.  It's really really amazing.  

The courses are a LOT of fun to race.  I am still terrible at the game, and the game is HARD.  Trust me, you don't have to be a good racer to enjoy this game.

The biggest issues I have with the game is that it does not explain much, and the interface could be a lot better.  For example, in career mode it isn't explained to you very well how car repairs work, and where and when you are allowed to fix your car.  You can hit a button on the controller for "Details" on a race, which brings up a menu with icons to show this, but even then it isn't obvious to a new player.  

I'm also not a fan of the storefront.  There are many "groupings" of cars, but the storefront doesn't really group them well, or explain what the difference is between the groups.  This likely isn't an issue for a rally fan, but for me it is confusing.  I'd also like to be able to see a list of cars I already own versus what is in the store.

I play the game using an XBox One controller on my PC, and it works great.  I have considered getting a wheel, but I am just not there yet.  The controller works great.

All of my issues with the game are in how it works when you are NOT racing.  When you are racing, it is superb.  The game is difficult, and I'll never be amazing at it, but it is a lot of fun.  There is a LOT of content for this game.  I've got quite a few hours in it at this point, and there are still stages that I am terrible at, and lots of cars that I haven't driven.  Between the base game and the content in the seasons and expansion pack, this game will keep you busy for a LONG time.

Review:

-The DLC scheme is pure garbage with recycled content from Dirt Rally:

All the hate they are getting from people regarding the DLC's is completely justified. Codemasters should feel ashamed when some bean counter thought of this as a great way to make extra money. This would be acceptable if the DLC's brought unseen content to the game (just go to CMR 2.0 and check what a wide variety of cars are available there, even if they were useless, they were fun), instead, they have cut stuff out of Dirt Rally 1.0 and added it as additional content in Dirt Rally 2.0 where it should have come with it in the first place. 

- What a proper DLC should look like:
1. Open online video sharing site (can't name it due to restrictions)
2. Search for Finnish amateur rallies
3. Take note as to what cars they are driving
4. Bring them to game (You are licensing most brands already \o/)
The game has some sort of economic model in it already, implementing amateur series rally would not be that hard where you advance, build, tune your cheap car to become a better machine, ultimately becoming eligible to enter high class rallies. 
To do this, you would need to borrow elements from other games, both new and old, but this is the only way to bring something new to a stale genre such as rally sims and attract new people.

-Career mode has integrated (recycled) elements from Dirt game (the most recent one), as well as the UI.
-Game engine is tweaked enough to feel like a new game, mostly in the lighting department:

Some random stutter can be observed during stages where scenes change quickly from empty to full of crowds and light sources. I assume this is an optimization issue because there is no chance in hell the game that looks like this should be that resource heavy.

- Sound is somewhat fine:
If Dirt Rally made shivers go down your spine when you heard that Audi Quattro scream or the Subaru Impreza with ALS roaring through the forest, there is no such feeling with Dirt Rally 2.0.
I can't quite put my finger as to why, others might disagree.

- Handling is more mature in this game than it was in it's predecessor. 
- The game is not as hardcore as the old one:

The stages appear to be created to be more forgiving. If you ever stepped your wheel of the track in Dirt Rally 1, you were fu****ed. In this game, you can take more aggressive trajectories through the corners and get away with it. Everything that should catch you doing that (be it a random ditch or a 1 meter long random wall in a middle of nowhere) is moved backward so you catch it only if you are very "arcady" with your driving. Or I`m just very lucky, who knows.

- The game does not feel alive, the atmosphere is not there

This has been the bane of rally sims since I remember. It just does not feel that alive and it does not create the atmosphere of rally. Sure, the technology has allowed to implement more "realisticly" animated crowds and light sources, cameras etc., but I feel that is is not enough. Someone needs to bring some new ideas on how to make the stage environment become more alive, more immersive. 
Of course - the game is supposed to simulate the handling and driving of cars, but if the environment get's left behind, no hyper-realistic physics models will save the game itself from being just - "meh, yeah, the cars drive good, but it get's rather repetetive and booring quickly"
I loved how they implemented that you could catch some other cars during stages in the previous Dirt games (Dirt 2, 3 and 4 I think), which might not be as realistic (cars in rally are launched with 2 minute buffers) but it could add more immersion that there is an actual Rally event happening.
The "random events" is not enough.

- Official World RX game:
Well, it couldn't have been more repetitive than it currently is, that is for sure, let me elaborate: You qualify for 4 rounds, 4 laps each. 
After qualification, you drive 2 times 6 laps to win.
Rinse and repeat, learn the tracks once and just grind.


TLDR:
Is this game worthy to wear 2.0 abreviation? Yes, but just barely.
If you are thinking if this game is worth it`s full price, it is not. Wait for sale for the mega super deluxe edition.
Not as hardcore as the previous game so it will be easier for casual drivers.
Horrendous DLC scheme with no signs of stopping.
I pat on the back of the people creating the game, thank you, for all your hard work, and I fully shame the financial department for becoming the same as majority of game companies

Let me just start off by saying that I have a love-hate relationship with Dirt Rally 2.0. My first experience with the game was getting the base version free with PS Plus when I used to be a console player, and initially I hated it. Granted I wasn't very experienced with the game, so every mistake I made in rallies, I kept cussing under my breath and just didn't find it fun. Now that I've nabbed the GOTY Edition while it was on sale on Steam and sunk a fair amount of time into it after getting some guidance on how to approach the game from my friends, I'm enjoying it a bit more, but I still have a fair amount of beef with the game.

What I do like about the game is that it feels pretty intuitive to drive on a pad (playing on an Xbox Series X controller here, don't have a wheel or room for one) even with the default settings. A bit of a shocker for a hardcore rally simulator, but as a result the driving experience feels really good. Actually tackling rallies in this game is a visceral experience that keeps you engaged as you blitz through dirt and tarmac roads with the co-driver guiding you every step of the way. Mistakes are especially punishing in this game, moreso than any rally game I've ever played in my life, but if you can put together a flawless run or even a close run against the AI or other players in a league you're doing, you'll feel like an absolute god. Cars and environment variety itself is a high point as well, with a huge majority of the boxes being ticked for car representation, as well as a whole host of different rallies around the world around a wide range of enviroments such as forests, deserts, snow and cliffside mountains.

I have problems with the rest of the game, however, specifically the career structure, a few game design decisions and the DLC model. Starting off, despite having sunk my teeth considerably into the career, I'm really not a fan of how the career is structured. Essentially there's five difficulty tiers for Career Rally and Rallycross; from easiest to hardest: Open, Clubman, Pro, Elite and Masters. Understandably you start on Open, which has the least amount of stages per rally, but it has you racing against pitifully slow AI. I do get it's supposed to settle you into the career, but the only form of challenge you'll be finding throughout your first championship is from making sure you survive the rallies at all. This could easily be solved personally by fine-tuning the AI difficulty to whatever you feel comfortable with while the "tiers" just determine how many stages per rally you're going to be doing, but alas, this isn't the case. Speaking of the career, the way championships are generated is completely random and is based on what DLC you own, meaning if you have the base game, you'll be stuck repeating the same six rallies over and over again in a different order. More variety in what rallies you'll be doing in the next championship can be achieved by having all the DLC, which is another problem in and of itself, but I'll be discussing that later... you also have Daily, Weekly and Monthly challenges to do as well, which you only have one shot at doing. No takebacks either, so if you make any mistakes, tough luck because you'll have to deal with it. But at the end of the day, I can't say I'm too big on how the career mode is structured personally, as more of a fan of a "traditional" racing game career mode that has a definitive start to conclusion. Maybe the best way to describe it is, it's more like a "service", akin to iRacing or Gran Turismo Sport, but for rallying... One more thing about the career, the fact that for a singleplayer experience, it requires you to be constantly online is very annoying.

I briefly touched on it last paragraph but I do understand that this game is supposed to be a hardcore rally simulator but sometimes it can get way too unforgiving. As I mentioned earlier, Daily, Weekly and Monthly challenges in the career (and I believe Leagues too) can only be done once, with no takebacks either, meaning you need to make your single shot count. If you're a perfectionist, it's more than likely you'll be kicking yourself if you screw up that one attempt because you feel you could've be able to optimize that run. This also applies to the Career Rally and Rallycross proper, but you have a slightly better safety net since it gives you five restarts per rally in that (although you can cheese it by quitting to the main menu and starting the stage over from there). Once again I get this is supposed to be a hardcore rally simulator but at the same time it gets to the point where it almost feels like the game actively taunts you for making mistakes since there's no do-overs. Feel free to give me shit for this and yell "LMAO GIT GUD LOSER LOLOLOL!!!1!" at me for saying this but there's a point where it gets a bit much...

Last main issue with the game is the DLC model. The best way to sum it up: if you get the base game, you're only getting half of Dirt Rally 2.0. That means, like I said before, you'll be stuck doing the same six vanilla rallies unless you have the DLC. Daily, Weekly and Monthly challenges may also require DLC rallies and cars as well so you'll be locked out of doing those if you're only playing the base game. From my research, a good chunk of the DLC is also content that was originally available from the beginning in Dirt Rally 1 (specifically all six of its rallies: Greece, Wales, Monaco, Germany, Finland and Sweden, as well as the RWD Group B cars, F2 Kitcars, and some of the Up to 2000cc rally cars) and Dirt 4 (Group B Rallycross). A bit scummy if you ask me, personally.

This last issue is a bit of a me thing personally, but while the actual rallying experience is very engaging, it's a bit of a double edged sword. It'll keep you very alert and on your toes, but it will keep you on edge and stress you out, for better or for worse. On one hand, you'll feel super satisfied when you manage to nail a stage and master the car you're driving on the dirt roads. But on the other, when you miscalculate corners, crash into fences and trees, plummet off corners or spin out, it's likely you'll be screaming profanities or cursing out the game, or at worst, you'll feel like you want to throw your controller at the monitor. But believe me, all that suffering is worth it when you can focus all your concentration into getting that one perfect run... and like I said before, you'll feel like an absolute god when you nail it.

So, would I recommend Dirt Rally 2.0? Depends. Are you a casual racing game fan. a perfectionist to a fault or one of those "angry gamer" types? Steer clear from this game and get Dirt 4 or 5 instead, you won't have any fun with this game at all. Are you a rally enthusiast, a hardcore racing game fan, a sim racer, or are you looking for a challenge? Then this is the game for you. Just... get the GOTY Edition (especially on sale), you'll be doing yourself a disservice if you only get the base game. And prepare to get your shit pushed in. A lot. You'll crash a lot on your first outings.

TL;DR - Dirt Rally 2.0 has great gameplay, wide variety of content, but is let down by a shoddy career mode that requires you to be always online, some game design decisions make the game more difficult than it already is (in a cheap way, not a challenging way) and the DLC model is pretty naff since it makes you pay for content already in Dirt 4/Dirt Rally and makes you feel like you're playing half the game if you've only got the base game.

[h2]Other[/h2]
As well as the new locations and cars the GOTY Edition also includes a bunch of extra starting money. All of the extra cars and a handful of cars from the standard game are unlocked from the start. This is nice as it really cuts down the amount of tedious grinding you have to do to save up for new cars and gives a lot more variety in the early stages of the game. The GOTY Edition also comes with a series of challenges based round the career of Colin McRae. These are really nice as it adds variety,  these challenges are not just about winning, they include goals like finishing without taking damage or finishing above a certain position when starting with specific damage.

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]
I think the extra tracks and cars are well worth getting the GOTY Edition. The more difficult question is should you still buy the original Dirt Rally as well as this game? I’d lean towards yes, it is not as polished as this game as this but you can get many more hours of gameplay out of it. Also I can see that these games are not going to appeal everyone so if you can pick up the original game for cheap in a sale you can save yourself the money of buying this one if it turns out to not be your cup of tea.

[h1]Review[/h1] 
My comments here are through the lens of what I thought about the original Dirt Rally which was that the driving experience was fantastic but it pandered too much to the hard core gamers and lacked the glue to make it into a great game.

So let’s start with the good. I cannot overstate how much fun the driving is in this game. There are so many different classic cars that are noticeably different to drive. In this game the weather and tyre wear seem to have a more significant effect. The tracks are nice and varied. The game looks and sounds gorgeous. The achievements are a bit more varied than the previous game which makes it a bit more fun to collect them.

Career mode was the main focus of the previous game but in this game I barely touched it. It is still too difficult and focused on grinding to unlock the tuned up version of the cars. It is however improved from the previous game. The levelling up of your crew is a bit nicer. The daily, weekly and monthly events are now done with the same cars you use in career mode. This makes the grinding for career mode much less tedious as you can have multiple events on the go at the same time and switch between them. Because you are racing against other people in daily, weekly and monthly events it is a much more level playing field. If you do a relatively smooth run with a few mistakes you will finish in the top 20-25% of a daily challenge against other people but dead last against the AI. It is way more satisfying to finish in the top 100 on a challenge against other people that it is to hopelessly thrashed by the arbitrarily difficult AI. There are a lot more of these events than the previous game too.

I really like the addition of Historic rally and FIA World Rallycross Championship modes. For me these were where the most of the fun was to be had. You skip all the tedium of career mode and can just get behind the wheel of all your favourite cars but with a nice sense of progression as you unlock more events. I just wish this section of the game was bigger and featured more of the extra content of the GOTY Edition.

A few other minor quibbles. I didn’t like the new co-driver I found him too animated in his speech, I preferred the previous less emotional, consistent directions but I got used to it. Still no Toyotas, I realise this is probably due to some boring licencing agreements but in my head it is because someone in the team is still holding a grudge from the 1995 WRC. Being able to set the name that appears on the car is a nice touch but why not make this work with the realistic liveries as well? In a similar vein it would be nice if the cars had decals specific to the different rally locations. I still think it would be nice to have more of the assists from Dirt 3 like the time rewind to make this accessible to more casual gamers. It would also be nice to have a bit of AI in the spectators. It does break the immersion when you crash and the spectators just stand there indifferent to their inevitable demise. I realise getting them to all jump out the way like in Driver San Francisco is a bit of an ask but they could at least react to the car.

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]
So there are a few things I would have done differently if I was in charge of this game but overall this has to be one of my favourite racing games.

You have to put yourself in the right frame of mind to succeed in this game. Colin McCrae’s mantra, “when in doubt, flat out” is great advice if you’re already a world class rally driver. For the rest of us, life is about showing up. The racer that drives at 8/10ths to survive is the one who shows up at the finish line for a decent time.

I love going into each stage blind and following the pace notes, but it’s worth burning a stage to learn how to control your car. Pick one with a couple hairpins. Chase a ghost. Get the front wheels to bite by dabbing the brakes so you can turn in. Turn off all the HUD elements except for the tachometer -- Seeing your time and position relative to the stage leader only encourages you to overdrive the car into a tree.

As I crest 100 hours of gameplay, I’m appreciating the nuance each vehicle offers and the design language of each locale. Front engine rear drive cars are easy to handle but force you to focus on weight transfer and feeding power in on corner exit. Mid-rear cars are a bit twitchy but give you better drive out of corners. The rear-rear Porsche has a big butt that likes to smack trees. And AWD cars allow you to rocket out of corners, make liberal use of the handbrake, and correct bad lines with a jerk of the wheel and much power.

I probably didn’t begin to memorize parts of the locales until around 70 hours in. Even now, I rely more on the pace notes than my memory. Allowing Phil’s pace notes to occupy a subconscious part of my short-term memory tends to scrub the stages from my brain upon completion. Each locale has a language, though; a set of corner types that you’ll keep seeing in different variations, a level of traction and road width that you must dial yourself in to. One event will have many 5 and 6 turns with big stops for square or hairpin turns. Others will have many flowing 3 and 4 turns. Argentina is almost nothing but hairpins and brief squirts of throttle.

DIRT Rally 2.0 is a very fun game, but is ABSOLUTELY NOT for someone who is just getting into racing games. As someone who has been playing racing games for about 15 years now, I am continuously challenged by this game. I rarely actually get upset at a game, but if any game can do it, it's this one.

I've found myself doing rally stages where I feel like i absolutely could NOT be going ANY faster, yet I am 8-14 SECONDS BEHIND FIRST! The game notifies you of this during your race, which is supposed to simply inform you of your current standing. But for me, I find myself trying to go even faster. Pretty much sealing my fate for the race. Not to mention you can only restart JUST A FEW TIMES. This means that if you crash, you could be seriously messing up your standings in the championship you're participating in, and could cost you hours of gameplay if you want to get first in every challenge.

I haven't discussed my main issue about this game, and it's hilariously simple; I ABSOLUTELY HATE THE CO-DRIVER VOICE. I'm surprised I haven't seen this elsewhere in reviews for this game, but I am shocked at just how awful the pace notes are for racing. The main reason for this is the way that the voice actor pronounces words. It's so frustrating to deal with while racing, and it really stands in the way of the whole experience.

For example, you'll be going ~80mph down a very tight dirt road, and will hear the co-driver suddenly say 

"5 Left into 6 right long-a into keep left over crest. 150-a into 4 right"

I'm sure you'll notice that behind a couple of words I've included a '-a'. This is because the voice actor for whatever reason pronounces certain words in the pace notes with an almost italian-esque 'a' at the end of them. For someone who is easily annoyed, this can be a bit frustrating, but the real issue with this is that it costs ACTUAL PRECIOUS METERS OF SPACE THAT YOU'RE DRIVING. I've literally completely OBLITERATED my car because of the actor taking too long to give me the appropriate pace notes. I've changed when the notes are read aloud, but it usually doesn't help, as the frequency in which the words are said, and the spaces in between them, are not changed. 

In the original DIRT Rally, which I'll admit I haven't played much of, there is a different voice actor for the co-driver, which is much more articulate, and is A LOT better than the one in this game. It completely astonishes me how annoyed I get about this, but now you've read my reasoning...

Other than these things, this game is seriously fun. The handling model is unforgiving, but it makes it feel as though you're behind the wheel of an unpredictable and hardcore rally car (or whatever other vehicle you're driving). The stats and driving characteristics of each vehicle are shockingly different to one another, even within the same class. This makes it so car shopping in this game is quite difficult! You have to find a vehicle you're comfortable with before taking it on a championship. I've made the mistake in-game of purchasing vehicles I couldnt afford, and then being too terrible at the game to even properly drive them. Lesson learned!

If you're a fan of racing games, I seriously do recommend this game. It's exciting and seriously makes you feel like a driving god as soon as you can barrel down tight snowy roads in a 50-year-old $500,000 dollar rally car at 80mph... and not die! It can get your heart rate up when you're inches away from falling off of a mountain while drifting along a tight corner. I've had a seriously fun time, regardless of how absolutely frustrating it can be at times.

Dirt Rally 2.0 is a game that truly lives up to its name, providing players with an adrenaline-fueled, white-knuckle experience that is as exhilarating as it is infuriating. Developed by Codemasters, this rally racing game takes difficulty to a whole new level, leaving players grappling with frustration as they navigate treacherous tracks filled with unexpected obstacles.

One of Dirt Rally 2.0's standout features is its realistic physics engine, which accurately simulates the dynamics of rally racing. The feeling of sliding through gravel, the responsiveness of the steering, and the impact of each jump are meticulously crafted to offer a genuine rally experience. However, this attention to realism comes at a cost—namely, a steep learning curve that can leave even seasoned racing game veterans struggling to keep their cars on the track.

The tracks themselves are beautifully designed, winding through diverse landscapes ranging from dense forests to mountainous terrains. However, the picturesque scenery can quickly become an adversary, as tightly packed trees and unforgiving terrain turn what should be a scenic drive into a chaotic ballet of rolling vehicles. It's not uncommon for players to find themselves airborne one moment and careening into a tree the next.

The difficulty of Dirt Rally 2.0 lies not only in the precision required to navigate the tracks but also in the unpredictable nature of the obstacles. The game seems to revel in catching players off guard, with sudden turns, hidden jumps, and deviously placed trees conspiring to send your car spinning out of control. The frustration peaks when, after a particularly challenging section, a simple mistake sends your vehicle tumbling like a pinball, leading to a series of rolls that would make a gymnast jealous.

While some may appreciate the high stakes and the thrill of overcoming seemingly insurmountable challenges, others may find the difficulty level excessive and discouraging. The lack of a gradual difficulty curve may alienate casual players, leaving them feeling more like crash test dummies than rally champions.

In conclusion, Dirt Rally 2.0 is a rally game that lives up to its promise of delivering an intense and challenging experience. The realistic physics, stunning tracks, and heart-pounding moments make it a unique entry in the racing game genre. However, its unrelenting difficulty and penchant for turning a relaxing drive into a chaotic mess may not be for everyone. If you're up for the challenge and have a high tolerance for frustration, Dirt Rally 2.0 might just be the adrenaline fix you're looking for. Just be prepared for a fair share of rolling on the ground and colliding with trees along the way.

This simulator is nothing short of exhilarating. I am not exaggerating. I love it! I play using a Valve Index at 120hz and the feeling of flying blindly down a dusty track only knowing what's coming around the hill or corner because the guy next to me is reading it off of a piece of paper is just incredible. I got this on a sale and then upgraded it to GOTY because I loved it so much. I highly recommend you do the same if you don't know if you're going to like it or not. If you buy the GOTY afterwards you get all the DLC's just not another copy of the base game. Easy.

The graphics look great in VR and the sound quality is top notch which is important to me when spending time in VR. I want things to look and sound good because I find it to be more fun that way. The championships against AI are easy at first but the more you do the harder the AI gets. You'll go from winning events like I was to rarely winning any anymore. Why? Because the sim is quite difficult! But that's what makes it so fun. Between Assetto Corsa, Assetto Corsa Competizione, and this, this is by far my favorite just because of how much fun it is. I'll include some controller settings to make things a little easier.

There is a career championship mode or you can create your own custom champtionships. There's rally racing which is mostly rural rough terrain tracks with lots of curves and hills and there's rally cross with are tracks that have tarmac and gravel. There are a bunch of single player modes you can play I don't need to list them all you will be pleasantly surprised by the variety. But best of all are the daily, weekly, and monthly challenges. They offer a wide variety of events with various types of cars and maps. I like playing these because it takes the decision making out of the equation for me.

You get credits for fininshing events. You can use those credits to buy cars, upgrade your team, or repair the cars you bought and roughed up on the track. The sim comes with some free cars you don't need to pay to repair and you can use those to accumulate more credits to buy better cars with when you're just starting out.

Dirt Rally 2 is one of the must-play VR games in my opinion. Nothing comes close to the feeling of flying and drifting down those tracks knowing you're potentially one mistake away from flying off a cliff! But you know what I love most about it?

I do have one complaint: The new user experience is rough. The most obvious place to start, career mode, has limited restarts and finite resources and isn’t the best way to learn the ropes. Time trials, on the second page, are probably the best way to learn but there’s discoverability issues and even then you’re thrown in the deep end, potentially trying to learn on Argentina, one of the hardest stages.

Now of course the majority of the audience already know how these games work, know exactly what class of car they want to drive and there’s lots of excellent guides out there. But when I first started playing I didn’t and it was only due to grinding away in a strong belief I probably would like it that I got to a place where I could truly enjoy the game. I hate to think that others who would love the game never got to that point because there’s no clear tutorial or path to ease beginners into the game.

And just in case anyone misreads this: I don't want the game itself to be easier, just more clear about what the best way to learn how to play is.
